And that there is such a vast Collection of Waters lodged in the Bowels of the Earth, is confirmed by abundance of Observations. ji The Water of this vast Abyss the DoGtor asserts, doth: communicate with that of the Ocean, by means of certain Holes, Hiatus's or Cajins betwixt it and the Bottom of the Ocean: this and the Aby s he supposes to have one common Centre, around with the Water of both of them is placed; but so, that the ordinary Surface of the Abyss. snot level with that of the Ocean, nor at so great a distance from the Centre as that is, it being for the most part restrained and fed by the Strata of Eardslying upon it; but whereever those Strata's are broken, or so lax'and prose that Water can pervade them, there the Water of the Abyss doth ascend, fills up all the! amphiblestroidesorthetunicaretina.c: AMPHIBLESTROIDES, or the Tunica Retina, or Retiformis of the Eye, is a soft, white and slimy Substance; which is f named, because that being thrown in the Water it resembles a Net; it shoots from the very Centre of the Optick Nerve, and consists of the Medullar Substance of it, and expanding itself over the Vitreous Humour, is ex - tended. as far as the Ligamentum Ciliare, or the Ligaments of the Eye-lids: This Tunic, in thar it is whitish and of a marrowy Substance, seems to pole from the very marrowy and fibrous. Sub - ance of the were, an Expansion of Nervous Fibres, which are there gathered into one Bundle, into a Contexture made like a Net; and indeed if the whole Eye were taken for a Flower, growing, as it were, tothe Brain by the Stalk ofthe Optick Nerve, the Tunica Retina would be the very Flower itself, and the two other Tunicles, the Sc erotical and Choroides, be only in the Nature of a Stem. This Tunic seems to be the principal Organ of Sight, and receives the visible Bre cies within the Bed of the Eye, much after the same manner as a whited Wall, or a piece of white Paper in a darkened Chamber, receives and represents the visible Species which are intro - mitted thro a little Hole: See Camera Obfcura.

Whether among the Operations Natural Bodies one upon another, there be any such thing as Artra tion, properly so speaking, is a Question that hath been much debated among Philosophers: And perhaps mot of those E which the Ancients, not knowing so well the Causes of, did use to attribute to Aftrattion, may now be very well solved by Pridfion. See Fames Bern ali, de Gravitare 7 Ether is, Amferdam, 1683, in. 8 vo. However the Word is retained by. go Naturalists, and in particular, by the Excellent Sir Isaac Newton in his ragoo ia but without there determining any thing of the Quale of it, for he doth not consider things so much Physical as Mathematically. This therefore being premifed, he laysitdown asan'Axiom; That since A tion and Re-action are always med and directly contrary to each other; therefore if any thing Attract another, it is itself also as much attracted by that other thing 5 so sien in the largest and most " general, for the Conatus of one Body towards another, however it be caused. And ii Cor. 1. Prop. 58. he shews, s 1. That if two Bodies mutually do attract each other ( by which he means the same as gravitate towards one another) by Forces proportionable to their Distances, they will diatribe both about the common Cefiter of Gravity, and about one another Concent ri al Ellipses; and vice versa, if any Body to describe such Figures, their Gravitating Sue ee Forces are proportional to their DieS. 2, That if cox Am ie hag e oa lg portion al to the Squares of their Distances, tie will defetibe Beh about the common Center of Gravity, and also about one another, Coz tick Scions having their Umbilici in the Center about which the Figures are described; and vice versa, & e. 3. He demonstrates also, That any Particle of " Matter within the Superficies of any Sphere or Globe, is attracted: or gravitates by a Force proportional to its distance trom the Center; but with: out the Surface of the Sphere, by a Force proper - ional to the Square of its distance from the Center, Prop.. 73, 14 Lib. 1. Hence it will follow, he faith,. 1. That at equal Distances from the Center of eon ce Spheres, She Attratticn will be as the Sphere. a. And at any distance whatever, the AttraCtion is as the Sphere divided by the'Square of the Distance. 3. Which last holds also in the Attractions of towards. one another; f. e. the Attractions are as the attracting Globes divided by the Squares of were: ie tho? the Globes mutually attract each er. The Quantity of the Force of Area tion in all Bodies at equal Distances, is exactly proportion - able tothe Quantity of Matter in the At tra tin Body, as being inteality nothing but the Resale or Sum of the united Forces of all those single Particles of which it is composed. ATTRACTION. Sir / isaac Newton at the end of the Latin Edition of his excellent Book of Op -, ticks, Ou. 22. shews that of those Bodies which are of the same Nature, Kind, and Virtue, by how much less any Body is than another, the greater is its attractive Force, in proportion to its Magnitude. Thus tis found that the Magnstick A traction is stronger in a fall Loadstone, in proportion to its, Weight, than in a / larger: For the Particles of small Magnets, being nearer one to another, can more easily combine or join their Forces into one. Wherefore the Rays of Light, being the leat of a! l Bodies that we know, must needs have the greater and frongzft attractive Force; and how very strongly tho Particles d attract, may be collected by the following Calculation, The At tra - Sion of a Ray of Light, with regard to the Quantity of its Matter, is to the Gravity which any projected Body hath, in proportion to the Quantity of Matter in that Body:: in a Ratio compounded of the Velocity of a Ray of Light, to che Velocity of that projected Body, and of the oe yo a see EE uu E EEN NEEEEEeennsnes ur or Curvature of the Line which the Ray describes in the place of its Refraction, to rhe Curvature or Flexure of the Line which the said projected Body describes. That is, supposing the Inclination of the Ray, to the refracting Surface be the same sip that of the Horizon. And from this Proposition he Calculates that the Attraction of the Rays of Light is above 1 ooca 0 d 0 cc os 00 co a Thoufarid Millions of Millions of Times greater than the Force of Gravity on the Earth's Surface according to the Quantity of matter in each; and supposing Light to come stom the Sun thither in about seven or eight Minutes. And in the very Point of Conta of the Rays, their attracting Force may be yet much greater. Now such a prodigious Force of AttraSion in the Rays of Light cannot but have wonderful Ef seats in those Particles of Matter, with which they are joyned in the Composition of Bodies; - and must cause that those Particles attrap & one another, and that they ate moved variously among them - ves. Tis very probable therefore that the / mall Particles of Bodies have certain Virtues, Powers or y which SN a: may a & not only on the Rays of Light to att, Refled or In slot them, ee een on one another, in order to produce most of the Pi in Nature. Tis very well known that some Bodies do thus a & ononeanother by the Attrattions of Gravity, Mag - netifin and Ele fri city; And these Examples shew what the Reason and Order of Nature is, and make it very probable that there may be yet some other At tra tions, for Nature is very uniform and agreeable to ir self.: Now the Attraftions of Gravity, Magnetism and Ele & ri city, extend themselves to considerable Di - stances, and therefore are commonly observed and - taken notice of by every one. But " tis very possible that there may be marly others also, which are contain'd in such narrow Limits, and performed within such a little Distance, as yet to have escaped all our Observations. For when Sale of Tartar runs per deliquium or, diffolves into an Oil as the Chymifts call it, tis very probable that it is occasion'd by some Attraction which is mutual between the Particles of the Salr, and those of Water, which rove up and down in the Air in the Form of Vapour; and the Reason why common Salt, Nitre and Vitriol, don't run thus per deliquium, is because they are without any such AttraGions; and when Salt of Tartar hath drawn as mach Wat r out of the Air as its Quantity will bear, it draws no more, because when it's Saturated, the Attraction isat end. It mustee also from its attractive Force, that the Water thus imbibed by the Salt, cannot be Neste from it in Distillation, but by avery violent Heat; whereas, Water will usually distill off with a very easy Hear, from other things. Tis much the same thing with Oil of Vitriol, which till it is Saturated with it, attracts the Moisture of the Air in very considerable Quantity, and afterwards parts with it with great Difficulty. And when Oyl of Vitriol and ater being mingled together in the same Vessel, grow so hor, sit is known they will do, it appears plainly by that Hear, that a. very great Motion is excited in the Particles of the two Liquors; and from that Motion it appears that their Particles in mingling Coalesce with a great Force and Impe - tufioty, and consequently attract or gravitate towards ne another with an accelerated Motion. Thus A YT also when Aqua fortis, Spirit of Vitriol or Nitre, or any other corrosive Menffruum diffolves Filings of Iron or any other Metal with Heat and Ebullition; tis plain that the Acid Particles of the Menfruum axcra & t and rush upon those of the Metal with very great Force, enter into their Pores with violence, and disjoin or separate the small Corpuscles of which the Metal is composed, one from another; tho the Particles of the Acid Menffruum are drawn off at first when they are made by a moderate Hear, yet after their Union they with the Parts of the Metal, cannot be drawn off as yet by Distillation, but by a. most intense and violent Heat. When Spirit of Vitriol? poured upon common Salt or Nitre, makes an Ebullition and Coalefces with the Salt; and when after this, if the Compost be distilled, a Spirit of Salt or Nitre will be drawn off much easier than without such a Mixture; it shews plainly that the Fixt Alkali of the Sale At tra ts the Acid Spirit of the Vitriol much more strongly than it, doth its own Spirit, and because it cannot retain them both, it parts with its own Spirit freely. When Oil of Vitriol is distill'd from an 2 4 Weight of Nitre, and from both is drawn off a Compound rete Nitre, and that Spirit is poured upon half its Weight of Oil of Cloves, of Car away - Seed, or any ponderous Oil distill'd from vegetable or animal Bodies, or upon Oil of Turpentine, mix'd with a little Balsam of Sulphur to thicken it; when in any of these Mixtures an actual Flame will be produc'd, " tis apparent that the Particles of the Spirit and Oil must ruth towards one another with a strong accelerated Motion, and struggle and fight with a most violent Force and Impetus. " Tis the same thing when that compound Spirit is poured upon well rectified Spirit of Wins, for a Flame will immediately arise on their Mixture. The Pulvis fulminans, as they call it, which is compos'd of Sulphur, Nitre and Salt of Tartar, goes off with a more quick and violent Explosion then even Gun-powder it self. The Acid Spirits of the Sulphur and the Nitre rushing together with such Violence, that all the Parts of the Powder are rarified, as it were, at once and all together, Thus also common crude and impure Brimffone ir self, if it be powder'd and mingled with an equal Weight of Filings of / ron or Steel, and with a little Water'be made up into thick Paste, like Dough, the Sige will a & so upon the Iron, thac in five or fix Hours time, the Mass will grow so hot as not to bear handling, and at last will plainly burn and emit a Flame. Now from all these Experiments, and from the Consideration of the great Quantity of Super that there is in the Earth, and of the great Heat of the inner Parts of it, from the hot Springs, the burning Vilcanos, the Fire Damps and burning Exhalations that are found in the Bowels of the Earth; from the Considerations of Earthquakes, Whirkwinds, and the wonderful Convulsions that the Sea is sometimes put into; we may understand, That the Particles of Bodies, before at Reft ( and tis the same thing also in all Fermentations, c.) may be and are put into most violent Motions, by some Principle of very great Force and A tivity, which yet doth not discover it self till the Parts approach and com very near one another; but that they do then attracts one another with great Force and Rapidity, and thereby produce their wonderful Effects, Again, when Oil of Tartar per deliqnium is poured upon the Solution of any Metal, there isa Precipitation of the Metalline Particles produc'd, which which all fall down to the Bottom of the Vessel; From whence it appears, the Liquor are more ly attrap & ted by those of the Oil of Tartar than by those of the Metal, and by that Attraction are precipitated down from the Liquor: So also when a Solution of Iron in Aqua Fortis will dissolve Cadmia, and Pre ie its Iron; when a aerie oabiosion will dissolve Iron, and let ee ee depart &c. this seems to rel plainly, that the ne Particles are mote strongly attracted by those of the Metal that they diftelve, than by those of that which is let go. When we find that those Menstruums which will dissolve one Kind of Metal or mix'd Body, won't touch another, it must be attributed to the Attraction that there is between the Particles in some Cafes, and there being no such in the other. And in the general it is owing to this Principle, that Heat, according to Ariffotle's Definition of it, doth congregate or together homogeneous Things, and [ separate those which are of a [ heed Nature: After this he ihews how on this Principle, and by the Help of Chymical An ass, to come to the Knowledge of what Kind of arts natural Bodies are composed. The Reason why Drops of Water, or other liquid Body usually put ona spherical Form, he with, is also from the'mutual Attraction of their Parts; after the same Manner as the Earth and Seas make one round Body by the ritual At tra i - on. ox Gravitate n of their Parts., And because when Metals are diffolv'd in Acids, they attract but a small Portions the Menftraum to them, therefore he concludes, that their Force of At tra tion extends but a very little Way. And asin Algebra, when affirmative Quantities vanish and terminate, their negative begin: So in Mechanicks, where Attraflion ceases to exert it self, a Kind of repelling Force should such ed; and that there is in Nature such a Force, seems to follow from the Reflsftion and InfleStion of the Rays of Light; for in both these Cafes, the Rays arelrepel - de ee. without the 4 ores of the nr; oe Body. And the same Thing seems concludable from ne Emission of Light; for a Ray of it, as soon as it is shaken out of the lucent Body by the vibrating Motion of its Parts, and is gor without the Sphere of its Attraction, is propelled with a very great Degree of Velocity; aud the same Force which in Refletion serves to repel the Ray, now serves to emit it. The Production of Air and Vapours doth also shew, that there isa repelling Force; for those Particles which are forced out of the Bodies by Heat or Fermentation, as soon as ever they are ont of the Sphere of the Attraction of these Bodies, do immediately recede from it, and from another with great Force, and do avoid coming together again; so that sometimes they take up above a Million of Times the Space which they did before; when they were in the Form ofa Dense Body, which is so very great a Contraction and Expansion as is hardly conceivable, if the Particles of the Air be only ee, rimose and coiled up one within ano - ther, like the Tendrels of Vines, or Springs of Watches, as some have imagin'd: Nor indeed, twill any other Hypothesis account for this wonderful Phenomenon, but this of their being endu'd with a repelling Force, by which they mutually avoid one another, as well as the Bodies from whence they at first came. auriclecordis.c: AURICLE Cordis, are two Appendages to the Heart, seated at its Basis over the Ventricles s they are so called from some Resemblance that they bear to the Ears of a Man's Head. They ari: e from a long Basis, and end in an obtuse Point, thereby forming an obtuse Triangle. They are of the same Fabrick and use with the Ventricles over which they stand, being Muscles as they are, made up of the same order of Fibres, which are carried into opposite Tendons; whereof that at the Basis of the Heart is common to it and the Auricule, and the other nesses their upper part. The Right 4 uric ie is larger and osier than the Left. The Superfices of both is smooth when they are full, but wrinkled when empty, and more so in the Left than in the Right one. On being cut open they exhibit many He shy Columns running from the Urs Tendon to the Lower, and between them there are pretty deep Furrows or long Cavities, but fewer in the Bight Auricle than in the Left. They are dilated and contra ted in like manner as the Heart is, but at different times; for the Sy / tole of the Ventricles is at the same time with the Diastole of the Auricles and vice versa; so that the Auricles are receiving their Blood from the Veins, while the Ventricles are expelling theirs into the Arteries: But when the Ventricles are relaxed and empty in their Dia sto /, then the Auricles force the Blood into them by their Sy / tole. They are nourished by Branches of Arteries springing from the Coronoria, which Dr. Ruy ( ch ( who seems first to have taken notice of this) calls therefore Arteries Auriculares, and no doubt but they have Branches also of Veins to attend them. assesofaship.c: ASSES, of a Ship, are two round Holes under her Head or Beak, through which the Cables pass when she is-at Anchor. they fay a Ship hath a Bold Hawse, when the Holes are high above Water. A Fresh Hawse, is when there 1 s a Suspicion it the Cables are fretted in the Holes. To Fresh Hawse, is to lay new Pieces upon the Cable in the Hawse. They call it burning in the Hawse, when the Cable endures an extraordinary Stress. Clearing the Hawf, is untwisting the Cables, which, by reason of the Ship's winding, are intangled one with another.

The Stone is found in most of the Hills between Scar borough and the River of Tees in the County of York, and also near Prest on in Lancafbire; " tis of a bluish Colour, and will cleave like Corn / h Slate. The Mine which lies deep in the Earth and is pretty well moistened with Springs is the best. The dry Mine is not good, and too much Moisture cankers and corrupts the Stone, making it nitrous. In this Mine are found . several Veins of Stone call'd Daggers, of the same Colour but not so good. Here are found those also which are commonly call'd Snake-Stones. For the. more convenient working of the Mine which sometimes lies 20 Yards under the Surface or Cap of the Earth ( which must be taken off and barrow'd away) they begin their Work on the Declivity of a Hill, where they may be also well furnish'd with Water. They dig down the Mine by Stages, to save Carriage, and so throw it down near the Places where they calcine it. The Mine before it is calcin'd, being expos'd to the Air will moulder into Pieces, and yield a Liquor whereof Copperas may be made: But being calcin'd it's fit for Alum; as Jong as it continues in the Earth, or in Water, it yemainsan hard Stone. Sometimes a Liquor will issue out of the Side of the Mine, which by the Sun's Heat is turn'd into natural Alu. The Mine is calcin'd with Cinders of New-Castle Coal, Woods and Furzes; he Fire made about two Foot and thick, two Yards broad, and ten Yards long. Betwixt every Fire are Stops made with wet rubbish; so that any one or more of them may be kindled, without Prejudice to the reft. After, there are 8 or 10 Yards Thickness of broken Mine laid on this Fewel, and 5 or 6 of them so covered; then they begin to kindle the Fires, and as the Fires rife towards the Top, they still lay on fresh Mine: So that to what Height you can raise the Heap, which is oftentimes about 20 Yards, the Fire without any farther Help of Fewel, will burn to the Top stronger than at the first kindling, so long as any Sulphur remains in the Stones. In cacao site Stones, the Wind many times does hurt, by forcing the Fire too quickly thr the Mine, leaving it black and half burnt; and in " others, burning the Mine too much, leaving it red, But where the Fire passes softly and of its own Accord, it leaves the Mine whole, which yields the best and greatest Quantity of Liquor.. The Mine thus calcin'd is put into Pits of Water supported with Frames of Wood, and ramm'd on all Sides with Clay; They are about ten Yards Jong, 5 broad, and 5 deep, and fet with a Current that turpeth the Liquor into a R ry, from whence tis pumpt into another Pit or Mi So that every Pit of Liquor, before it comes to boiling, is panes into four, several Pits of Mine; and every Pit of Mine is steeped in four several Liquors before it be thrown away; and the das pi being always of the fresh Mine. This Mine thus steeped in each of the several Liquors 24 Hours, or thereabouts, is of course four Days in passing the four several Pits from whence the Liquors pass to the boiling-House. The Water, or Virgin Liquor often gains in the fir Pit, two Pounds Weight; in the second it increase th to five Pounds, in the third to eight Pounds, and in the last Pit which is always fresh Mine to twelve Pounds; and so in Proportion aca cording to the Goodness of the Mine, and its being well calcin'd. For sometimes the Liquors passing the four several Pits, will not be increas'd to above fix or seven Pounds Weight, and at other times above twelve Pounds; seldom holding a con fant Weight one Week together: Yet many times Liquor of seven or eight Pounds Weight produces more Allum than that of ten or twelve Pounds Weight, either through the Badness of the Mine, or its being ill calcin'd, which is the usual Reason. And if by passing the weak Liquor thro another Pit of fresh Mine, you bring it to be ten or twelve Pounds Weight, yet you shall make less Allum with it, than when ic was but eight Pounds Mine will be most Nitre and Slam, which poisons the good Liquors, and diforders the whole House, till the Slam be ieer off, That which they call Slam, is first perceived by the Redness of the Liquor when it comes from the Pit, occasion'd either by the Badness of the Mine, or more usually its being over or under calcin'd, which in the Settler finks to the Bottom, and there becomes a muddy Substance,. and of a dark Co - Jour. That Liquor which comes whites from the Pits is the best. When a Work is first begun, they make Aim of the Liquor only that comes from the: Pits of Mine, without any other Ingredients. and so might continue, but that it would spend so much Liquor as not to " pee Cost. t Kelp is made of a Sea-weed call'd Tangle, such as comes to London in. Oyster Barrels. It grows on Rocks by the Sea-side, between high and low Water Mark. Being dry'd it will burn and run like Pitch; when cold and hard; tis beaten to Athes, steeped in Water, and the Lees drawn off to two Pound Weight or thereabouts. Because. the Country People who furnish the Work with Urine, do sometimes oer it with Sea-Water, which cannot be discover'd they try it, by putting some of it to the boiling Liquor; For then if the Urine be Genuine it will work like Yeast put to Beer or Ale; but if mingled, it will stir no more than so much Water. They observe that the best Urine for that Purpose, is such as comes from poor laboring People who drink but little strong Drink.: The boiling Pans are made of Lead, nine Feet long, five broad, and two't deep, fet upon Iron Plates about two Inches thick; which Pans are commonly new. Cast, and the Plates repair'd five times in two Years. When the Work is begun, and Ad ium once made, then they save the Liquor which comes from the All un, or wherein it shoots, which they call the Mothers, with this they fill? of the Boilers, and ut in of the fresh Liquor which comes from the Pics Being thus sill'd up with cold Liquor; the Fires having been never drawn out, it will boil again Weight. For what it gains from the last Pit of y Weight, na it will be 36 Pound Weight. Then is put in - about two ight, which will reduce the which it lands about two Hours, and'in tha time most of the Nitre and Slam sink to the tom. 9 q-we - This Separation is made by the help of the Kelp Lees, for when the ate Boiler consists of Green Liquor drawn from the Pits, it is of pow -. er strong enough to cast off the Slam and the Nitre; but when the Mothers are us'd, the Kelp Lees. are needful to make the said tion. are f Next the said Liquor is scooped out of the Settler into a Cooler, made of Deal Boards, and xamnrd with Clay. Into this is put 20 Gallo or more of the Urine, according to the G or Badness of the Liquor, for when the Liquor is Red and Nitrous, the more Urine is requir'd. - Inthe Cooler, the Liquor in temperate Weather stands four Days; the second Day the Allum begins to strike, gather and hardengabout the Sides, and at the bottom of the Cooler. If the Liquor should stand above four Days, then it would turn to Copperas. The Use of the Urine is as well to cast off the Slam, as to keep the Kelp Lees from hardening the Allum too much. In hot Weather the Liquor will bea Day longer in cooling, and the Allum in gathering, than in temperate Weather. But in Frost, the Allan shoots or strikes too soon, not giving time soothe Nitre and Slam to sink to the bottom, whereby re By mingl'd with the Alum, This produces double the Quantity, but being foul tis consumed in washing. When the Liquor hath stood four Day in the Cooler, than that call'd Mother, is cooped into a Cistern, the Alum " remaining on the Sides and Bottom; and from thence the Mothers are Pumpt back into the Boilers again: So that every five Days the Liquor is boil'd again, until it evaporate er turn into Allum or Slam. The Allum taken from the Sides and Bottom'of the Cooler, is put into a Cistern and washed with Water, that they use for the same Purpose; being about 12 Pound Weight, after which it is Roached as Follows. Being washed, it is put into another Pan with a ity of Water, where it Melts and Boil sa little; then tis cooped into great Cask, where it com - monly flays 10 Days, and is then fit to take down for the Market. abricklands.c: ABRICK Lands, are Lands given tothe Rebuilding, Repair, or Maintenance of Cathedrals, and other Churches, and mentioned in the Act of Oblivion, 12 Car. 2. c. 8. Formerly every one almost gave by his Will something, more less, to the Fabrick of the Cathedral, or his Parith Church, and these were called Fabrick Lands; and by the Saxons, Timber Lands.

aconglomerategland.c: AConglomerate Gland is composed of many little Conglobate Glands all tied together, and wrapt up in one common Tunicle or Membrane. Sometimes all their Du ts unite and make up one common Pipe, thro which the Liquor of all of them runs, as the Pancreas and the Parotides do. Sometimes the s uniting, form several Pipes, which only communicate with one another by cross Channels; and such are the Breasts, Others again have several Pips without any Communication with one another, of which Sort are the Glandule Lachrymales, and the Proftata. And a fourth Sort is, when each little Gland hath its own Excretory Duct, thro which it tran mits its Liquor to a common Bason, as in the Kidneys.: As to the Manner how the several Fluids, after they are form'd in the Blood, are separated from it inthe Glands; it depends ( as Dr. Keil thews, An, Secret, p. 82.) entirely on the Figure and Structure i ee Glands, which therefore must first be iewrgge 5 Truth, when plain co 8 evident, doth of itself dispel all false Opinions; the true Stru ture of the Glands ak ag demonftraa ted, there will be ne Occasion to refute the Dotirine of Ferments, nor the Hypothesis of Tubes differing as to the Figures of their Orifices; both which have several Times been demonstrated to be false. That the Glands are nothing but Conyolutions of mall Arteries, the greatest and most accurate Anatomists of this Age, Malpighi, Bellini, end Nuch, have discover'd, And indeed, that all the Vessels of the Body, in which the Liquors are continually moving, can have no other than a Cylindrical or Conical Form, is demonstrable from the Nature of Fluids, whose Pressure is always perpendicular to the Sides of the Vessel contain ing them, and equal ar equal Heights of the Fluid. If therefore the Sides of the vessels are fof, and equally yielding every where, ( as are all the Tubes in the Body of a Fetus) they must, by the Pressure of their contained Fluid, be equally every where distended; and consequently the Section of such a Vessel, perpendicular to its Axis, must be a Circle; and therefore the Vessel must be either concave Cone or Cylinder, or at least such a Fig are whose Transverse Section, normal to the Axis, must be a Circle. The Circular Orifices therefore of the Glands can only differ in Magnitude; and all Sorts of Particles, of a lesser Diameter than that ys 9 rice GLA - Orifice of the Gland, may enter it: So that without some further Contrivance, that Fluid which contains the biggest Particles, must likewise consist of all the Particles of all the other Secretions; neither could any Fluid thicker than the Blood be separated from it, because of the qe Proportion of the Aqueous Fluid, whose Particles r than any other, and invisible to Microscopes, must enter all the Glands, and be mix'd with the secerned Fluid. Now how this Inconvenience may be pre'vented, and how the Particles of any Size may either be separated by themselves, or with any stigeed Portion of the Aqueous Fluid, or of other lesser Particles, I shall endeavour to thew. K Aw Suppose then 4 B to be a mall evanescent Artery, and that the Particles of the least Size were to be separated from the reft. E From the Side of the Artery must arise the Gland or Tube C K, whose Orifice at is such as is capable of admitting only Particles of the Jeaft Size, together with the Aqueous Fluid: These therefore will be separated from all the other Particles " of the Blood, and the Tube C K. being a Cylinder, they will pass to its further End K, which is supposed to be the Excretory Da t of the Gland.: If the Quantity of the Aqueous Fluid, separated with the least Particles, must be diminith'd, that such a Fluid as is requisite may pass through the Excretory Duct K, from the Tube C K; you must imagine, that several other smaller Canals o out, as at D, E, F, and G, whole Orifices are ( o small, that they admit no other Particles, be. sides those of the Aqueous Fluid, co pass through them; and therefore as the least Particles, together with the Aqueous Fluid, pass along the Tube C K, the Aqueous Fluid must constantly be diminished; and the Quantity of the least Particles still remaining, they can pass no where but through the Excretory Duct at K: And this Diminution of the Aqueous Fluid will always be according to the Number of the Canals, D, E, F, G, that is, in Proportion to the Length of the Tube CK. And therefore, according as the Gland is longer or shorter, so the more or less Aqueous Fluid will pass through the Orifice of the Excretory Duct at K; and consequently, the secreted Fluid, on this Account, be Thicker or Thin. ner. If the Particles of a middle Size, between the biggest and the least, are to be drawn off from the reft of the Blood: Let the Orifice tthe Gland C be just so big as to admit those Particles, and nor any other of a larger Size. These Particles therefore, with the Aqueous Fluid, and all better Particles, will pass through the Orifice C; bur if the Canals D, E, F, G, are big enough to receive all the other Particles, and too little to admit those that are to be separated, it is evident, thar those Particles must arrive at the Excretory Duct K, with what Proportion of Lesser Particles is required. And thus we fee how any Sort of Particles may be drawn off, either by themselves, or mixed with any others, in any Proportion: And this is done in the most simple manner, only by Arteries; for CK is only a smaller Artery, either Straight, Spiral, or otherwise contorted, and D, E, F, and G, are again Arteries smaller than it; and if any of these are so mall as only to admit Particles of Serum, they will constitute Lymphatick Vessels, From whence it is, that we find Lymphedu ts arising in great Numbers from those Glands thac separate thick Humours; as from the Testicles, Liver, &c.
